name: Rimonabant (Acomplia)

lead: Rimonabant was an oral prescription drug for obesity that blocked the cannabinoid-1 receptor, the pathway involved in THC-driven appetite. In large trials it produced greater weight loss than placebo alongside diet and exercise.
It was approved in the EU in 2006 and rejected by the FDA in 2007. It was withdrawn from the market worldwide after psychiatric adverse events were reported.

paras: It acts as an inverse agonist at CB1 receptors in the brain and body, which reduces the reward and appetite signaling driven by the endocannabinoid system.

Trials and post-marketing data linked it to depression, anxiety and suicidal ideation, which led the EMA to recommend suspension in October 2008. It is no longer legally marketed in the EU, Brazil or India and was never approved in the US.

lead: Rimonabant, sold as Acomplia (and Zimulti), is an oral anti-obesity drug that blocks the cannabinoid-1 (CB1) receptor. It was developed by Sanofi-Aventis and was the first CB1 inverse agonist approved anywhere. [1][2]

In the large Rimonabant in Obesity (RIO) trials, people taking 20 mg a day alongside diet and exercise lost more weight than those on placebo, with improvements in waist circumference and lipid measures. [3][4][5][6] The European Commission approved it in 2006, but the US FDA did not approve it, and it was withdrawn worldwide in late 2008 after psychiatric adverse events, including depression and suicidal ideation, were reported. [2][6]

Rimonabant matters to appearance and fat-loss discussion mainly as a cautionary history of a prescription weight-loss drug. No community material about its use for cosmetic purposes was identified, so this article covers its medical record.
infobox: Withdrawn; never approved in the US [2]

paras: Rimonabant was approved in the EU for adults with a body mass index above 30, or above 27 with risk factors such as type 2 diabetes or dyslipidaemia, as an adjunct to diet and exercise. [2] It was also studied for smoking cessation, type 2 diabetes, fatty liver disease and cardiovascular risk reduction. [1][7]

The RIO program comprised several randomized, placebo-controlled phase III trials. In RIO-Europe, patients with obesity or overweight with comorbidities were randomized to rimonabant or placebo for one year, and weight and cardiovascular risk factors were measured. [3] RIO-Lipids (1,036 patients with dyslipidaemia) and RIO-North America (3,045 patients, two years) reported greater weight loss on the 20 mg dose than on placebo, along with changes in waist circumference and metabolic markers. [4][5]

A 2007 meta-analysis of randomized trials examined both efficacy and safety of the drug and reported that the weight benefit came with a higher rate of psychiatric adverse events. [6] A separate randomized study examined overweight or obese patients with type 2 diabetes. [8] Reviews comparing obesity drugs, including a 2007 BMJ meta-analysis, placed rimonabant alongside orlistat and sibutramine. [9][10]

In the trials submitted to regulators, depressive disorders or mood alterations occurred in up to about 10 percent of participants and suicidal ideation in about 1 percent. [2] In Europe the drug was contraindicated in people with psychiatric disorders including clinical depression. [2] Nausea and upper respiratory tract infections were very common, and anxiety, irritability, insomnia and gastrointestinal effects were common. [2]

The CRESCENDO outcomes trial, which enrolled over 18,000 participants, was terminated, and its published registration lists it as terminated. [11] Wikipedia reports that psychiatric events were seen in more than 30 percent of patients in that trial. [2]

Rimonabant blocks CB1 receptors in the brain and peripheral tissues. Animal work found that CB1 blockade produced a lean phenotype and resistance to diet-induced obesity, which was the rationale for testing it in people. [3] Wikipedia also notes it acts as a mu-opioid receptor antagonist. [2]
It is metabolized in the liver by CYP3A4 and is highly protein bound. Its elimination half-life is reported as 6 to 9 days at normal body mass index and about 16 days when BMI exceeds 30. [2]

Rimonabant (SR141716) was discovered by Sanofi in the 1990s as a selective CB1 antagonist, following identification of the CB1 receptor and its endogenous ligands. [1] Sanofi-Aventis submitted it to the FDA in 2005. [2]

The European Commission approved it on 21 June 2006. [2] In June 2007 the FDA advisory committee voted against recommending approval, the application was deemed not approvable, and the company cancelled resubmission plans. [2] In October 2008 the European Medicines Agency recommended suspension, concluding that risks including serious psychiatric problems outweighed benefits; Sanofi-Aventis suspended sales worldwide, and the EU marketing authorization was withdrawn in January 2009. [2]

Rimonabant was approved in the EU and in Brazil (April 2007) but has been withdrawn from those markets, and it was never approved in the United States. [2] India banned its manufacture and sale in 2009. [2]

Rimonabant has been the subject of renewed small trials in spinal cord injury and stroke walking recovery, registered between 2021 and 2026. [12][13] Other planned phase III trials in fatty liver, prediabetes and diabetes were terminated. [11][14][15]

Human trials include RIO-Europe, RIO-Lipids and RIO-North America, which tested weight and cardiometabolic effects in overweight and obese adults. [3][4][5] A 2007 meta-analysis pooled the published randomized trials for efficacy and safety. [6] A study in type 2 diabetes tested the drug in that population. [8] Registered trials in atherosclerosis imaging, prediabetes, fatty liver and cardiovascular outcomes were terminated. [11][14][15][16] A network meta-analysis of smoking-cessation pharmacotherapies also included rimonabant. [7]
